# Summary of the 2001 Manifesto

This manifesto presents a programme centred on transferring power from government to individuals, families, and local communities, emphasising "common sense" as its guiding principle.

## Family and Education
The document proposes tax cuts for families with young children, including increased child tax credits and allowances for single-income households. On education, it advocates giving schools independence from central bureaucracy, allowing headteachers control over admissions and staff rewards, enabling successful schools to expand, and creating "Progress Centres" for disruptive pupils. For higher education, it proposes raising the income threshold for student loan repayments and creating university endowment funds.

## Crime and Justice
The manifesto pledges to increase police numbers, reduce bureaucratic burdens on officers, and establish more secure training centres for persistent young offenders. It proposes "honesty in sentencing" where criminals serve their full court-given sentences, mandatory imprisonment for those selling drugs to minors, and enhanced victims' rights throughout the justice process.

## Economy and Taxation
Economic proposals include £8 billion in tax cuts funded through government efficiency savings, targeting families, pensioners, savers, and motorists. The document commits to reducing regulation on businesses through annual "regulatory budgets" and opposes joining the euro currency. It emphasises transparent economic management and lower public spending growth.

## Healthcare
For the health service, the manifesto proposes a "Patient's Guarantee" establishing maximum waiting times based on clinical need, removing political interference from hospital management, restoring authority to ward sisters, and allowing patients to choose their hospital. It would remove tax penalties on private medical insurance.

## Pensions and Elderly Care
Proposals include raising personal tax allowances for pensioners by £2,000, increasing the basic state pension (with higher increases for over-75s), abolishing compulsory annuity purchases at age 75, and enabling younger workers to opt for funded private pensions.

## Europe and Foreign Affairs
The document advocates remaining in the European Union while opposing further integration, maintaining the national currency, and renegotiating treaties to preserve parliamentary sovereignty. It supports NATO, opposes a separate European military structure, and proposes stricter asylum procedures including secure reception centres.

## Local Government and Rural Affairs
The manifesto pledges to abolish regional development agencies, devolve power to local councils, protect green spaces, and implement recovery measures for rural areas affected by disease outbreaks. It proposes cutting fuel taxes and rural business rates.

## Constitutional Reform
Proposals include allowing only English MPs to vote on England-only matters, strengthening parliamentary scrutiny, reforming the upper chamber to include elected elements, and reducing the overall number of politicians.
